one_liner: Nim getdents64/openat tree walker (cligen/dents) whose find, ls -R and du demos claim 1.4-4.5x over GNU tools.
what_it_does: cligen is mainly a Nim CLI-generator library; its cligen/dents module adds a recursive file-tree walker, forPath, written as a template: you pass code blocks for each entry, before recursion, after recursion and on failure. The same file builds a small multi-command demo (find, dstats, ls1AU, lss1AU) that prints paths or ls -1AUR / ls -s1AUR style listings, and c-blake/bu builds du, rr, newest and other tools on it. It is not a drop-in find: there is no expression language. You get a callback-style walker plus a few fixed-format printers.
how_it_is_fast: On Linux it calls getdents64 through syscall() into a 4066-byte buffer, which skips the fstat that opendir/fdopendir does per directory. It descends with openat/fstatat (statx) relative to the parent fd, so the kernel never sees full paths. It trusts d_type and opens directories optimistically with O_DIRECTORY instead of lstat-ing each entry. By default it treats a short getdents read as end-of-directory, which saves one getdents call per directory. An optional -d:batch build sends each directory's statx calls through the author's out-of-tree sys_batch kernel module; the author says this adds about 1.25x more.
when_to_use: Nim programs that must walk large local trees (ext4/xfs/btrfs/tmpfs) and want per-entry, pre- and post-directory hooks with the open dir fd and statx data available for *at() calls
Replacing a simple 'find DIR' / 'find -print0' or 'du -s' in scripts that run often on hot-cache local trees, where per-syscall overhead dominates
Tools that need post-order aggregation (du-like totals, rm -rf like bu/rr) without building path strings for every syscall
Linux x86-64 or similar; it also builds on BSDs through the libc fdopendir/readdir path, but the getdents64 speedups are Linux-only
when_not_to_use: NFS, sshfs or other FUSE/network file systems with default settings: the early-EOF shortcut can stop reading a directory after a short getdents read and silently drop entries (the source says 'Sadly, fails on sshfs/NFS/etc.'). Pass --eof0 / eof0=true there; bu du hard-codes eof0=false, so it cannot be made safe
Very deep trees: each level holds an open fd and EMFILE/ENFILE silently ends that subtree (recFailDefault discards them). It is depth-limited by ulimit -n, unlike GNU find's fts
When you need find predicates (-name, -newer, -exec, -prune) or exact GNU ls/du output; the demos print fixed formats and du drops several options
Cold-cache or many-core NVMe walks: it is single-threaded, while parallel walkers such as fd or minifind may win there; no cold-cache numbers exist
Non-Linux targets that care about speed: the getdents64 path, batch mode and the statx timestamps are Linux-specific

integration.form: module (Nim source, part of the cligen nimble package)
integration.dependencies: none beyond the Nim stdlib and libc; optional out-of-tree c-blake 'batch' kernel module and headers for -d:batch
integration.min_toolchain: Nim >= 1.4.0 per cligen.nimble (the nimble file warns that helper modules may need newer Nim); C backend
integration.platforms: Linux (getdents64 fast path; statx used only if the build host has /usr/include/bits/statx.h or the x86_64-linux-gnu copy, checked at compile time, else an fstatat fallback); other POSIX through libc fdopendir/readdir
integration.thread_safety: not documented; forPath keeps its state in template-local variables and uses the process-wide errno, so treat it as single-threaded
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: find prints the same path set for a plain recursive print on local file systems but has no predicates; ls1AU/lss1AU emit a different output order; bu du is 'mostly compatible' with GNU du but drops time, max-depth and separate-dirs options and uses PCRE patterns

gotchas: Early EOF is on by default: eof0=false makes fdopendir set eeof=true, so any getdents read shorter than about 3.5 KB ends the directory. Commit 7559cff (2020-06-28) turned the earlier opt-in -d:dentsLocalFS build switch into this runtime default. The benchmarked find/ls runs therefore used a shortcut that is unsafe on NFS/sshfs.

By code reading (not run): ls1AU and lss1AU buffer each directory's names and print them in the post-recursion hook, so subdirectories are listed before their parents, unlike GNU ls -R. lss1AU's showLong prints label.dirname (libc dirname), so each header names the parent directory. Their timed outputs went to /dev/null, which hides both differences from ls -1AUR / ls -s1AUR.

bu du (by code reading): the binary -p/--peta scale returns 1 shl 40 (TiB) instead of 1 shl 50; --exclude only skips adding the matched path's size and does not prune the walk; eof0 is hard-wired false. cligen/statx's < and <= on StatxTs compare tv_nsec with the other side's tv_sec.
The '1.7x faster than BSD find|fd' figure was first written as '1.7x faster than FreeBSD find'. Commit ebb78e9 (2020-10-28) only added '|fd' to that comment, with no new number for fd.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick dents over fd or minifind when you are writing Nim, need a library hook (pre/post-order callbacks with the dir fd) rather than a CLI, and walk hot local trees single-threaded. Pick fd for find-style matching with ignore files and parallelism, and dumac for a parallel du on macOS; dents has no measured numbers on par with their hyperfine tables.
verified_claims_summary: Only one-line doc comments: find 2.75-4.5x faster than GNU find on /usr and 1.7x faster than FreeBSD find (fd added later to the same comment); ls1AU -r0 1.7-2.25x and lss1AU 1.45-2.0x faster than GNU ls -1AUR / ls -s1AUR --color=none to /dev/null; bu du '1.4-2x faster' walk than GNU du. No machine, kernel, file system, cache state, tool versions, Nim/C flags or script are given. The numbers date from 2020, cover the non-batch build with the unsafe-on-NFS early-EOF default, and the ls comparisons do not produce identical output.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-08-26, ISC, 584 stars) and easy to vendor as one Nim module plus cligen helpers. The speed claims are unreproducible 2020 comments, and the default early-EOF shortcut, silent EMFILE bottoming-out and the output differences found in ls1AU/lss1AU and bu du (code reading, not run) mean you should pass eof0=true on network file systems and not treat the demos as exact GNU replacements.
